title: Order Types
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/0/body: A **market order** means "fill this right now at the best price available." A market buy fills at the **Ask**, and a market sell fills at the **Bid**. **Execution** is almost guaranteed, but the **exact price** isn't.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/1/body: A **limit order** means "only fill at this price or **better**." A **buy limit** sits below the current price (so you buy cheaper), and a **sell limit** sits above it (so you sell higher). Your price is guaranteed, but the market might never get there.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/2/prompt: You hold Ethereum and it's at $3,000 right now. You want to sell if it reaches $3,200. Which order do you place?
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/2/explanation: Selling above the current price is a sell limit: it only fills when the price reaches 3,200 or higher.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/3/statement: A limit order might never get filled.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/3/explanation: If the price never reaches your limit level, the order just sits there waiting. You get a better price, at the cost of maybe missing the move.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/4/prompt: The trend is down, and you want to sell when the price comes back up to the "?" line. Which order should you place there?
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/4/explanation: The line is above the current price and you want to sell there, which means selling at a better price than now. That's a sell limit.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/5/body: When **speed** matters more (like getting out of a trade right away), go market. When **price** matters more, go limit. On many crypto exchanges, a limit order that waits in the order book counts as a **maker** order and usually pays a lower fee than a **taker** order.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/5/tip: In a thin market, a big market order can fill at a much worse price.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/6/prompt: The price is moving fast against your trade and you want out right now. Which order?
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/6/options/1: A limit order at a better price than now
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/6/explanation: When you need an instant fill, use market. A limit at a better price might never fill, leaving you stuck in the loss.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/7/pairs/1/mea: An order that waits in the order book
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/7/pairs/2/mea: An order filled instantly from the order book
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/8/prompt: EUR/USD is at 1.0850 right now. You want to buy if the price drops 30 pips. Drag the buy limit to the right spot.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/8/explanation: 30 pips below 1.0850 is 1.0820. A buy limit always goes below the current price and only fills at that price or better. A buy order above the current price would fill almost instantly.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/9/prompt: You placed a buy limit at 1.0820. Tap the candle where your order got filled.
lessons/orders-u1-l1/steps/9/explanation: This is the only candle whose low reached 1.0820. The buy limit filled right then, and the price climbed back up afterward.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/title: Buy Stop, Sell Stop and Pending Orders
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/0/body: A **buy stop** goes above the current price: "If the price goes **higher**, buy." A **sell stop** goes below it: "If it comes **lower**, sell." Its main use is entering on a **breakout** of a level, when you want the move to prove itself first.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/1/body: Orders that wait for a specific price are called **pending** orders. The simple rule: **limit = better price** (expecting a reversal) and **stop = move confirmed** (expecting it to continue).
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/1/example/row: Below price; expects a bounce up
Above price; expects a drop back
Above price; expects the rise to go on
Below price; expects the fall to go on
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/2/prompt: You only want to sell if support breaks. What's the order on the "?" line?
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/2/explanation: The line is below the current price and you want to sell if the price falls that far, which means selling as the move continues. That's a sell stop.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/3/prompt: Bitcoin is at $60,000 and its key resistance is $62,000. You only want to buy if resistance breaks. Which order?
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/3/options/3: A market buy right now at 60,000
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/3/explanation: Buying above the current price after a breakout is a buy stop's job. Traders place it a little above the level so a small touch doesn't trigger it.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/4/prompt: You only want to sell if gold's 2380 support breaks. Drag the sell stop to the right spot.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/4/explanation: A sell stop goes below the current price and triggers when the price falls, so a little under support (say 2377) makes sense: it only triggers on a real break. Right at 2380, even a small wick would fill you; one wick already dipped to 2379.8 and bounced back.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/5/statement: When the price reaches a stop order, it turns into a market order and may fill with slippage.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/5/explanation: A stop is just the trigger. Once it fires, it fills at the best price available. In fast moves, it can fill a few pips worse.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/6/body: A **stop-limit** has two prices: when the price hits the **stop**, a **limit** order gets placed. It protects you from bad slippage, but it might not fill. Pending orders also have an **expiry**: either until you cancel them yourself (**GTC**) or until a set time.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/7/prompt: You placed a buy stop at 1.0856. Tap the candle where your order was triggered.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/7/explanation: The first candle whose high reached 1.0856 is this breakout candle; the order turned into a market buy right then. The candles before it stayed below resistance.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/8/sentence: A ___ order buys above the current price, and a ___ order sells above the current price.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/8/explanation: Both sit above the current price: a buy stop to buy as the rise continues, and a sell limit to sell at a better price.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/9/prompt: Put the events of a buy stop order in order.
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/9/items/0: Place a buy stop above resistance
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/9/items/2: It turns into a market order
lessons/orders-u1-l2/steps/9/explanation: A buy stop waits until the price gets there. Then it fills like a market order, and a buy position opens.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/0/body: **OCO** (One-Cancels-the-Other) means two orders are linked: **when one fills, the other gets canceled**. Its most common use is setting a take profit and a stop loss at the same time on an asset you hold, for example on a crypto exchange.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/0/tip: In MetaTrader, a position's stop loss and take profit basically work this way.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/1/prompt: With an OCO, you set a take profit at 66,000 and a stop loss at 57,000. The price reached 66,000. What happens?
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/1/options/0: Take profit fills and the stop loss cancels itself
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/1/options/2: The stop loss stays active until you cancel it
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/1/explanation: That's the OCO logic: one fills, the other cancels. This way, after you sell, there's no leftover sell order that could fill later by accident.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/2/statement: With an OCO, you can place a buy stop above a range and a sell stop below it, so when either side breaks, the other order cancels.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/2/explanation: That's a common OCO use for range breakouts: whichever side breaks, that order fills and the other one cancels. Of course, a fake breakout is still possible.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/3/body: A **trailing stop** is a stop loss that **follows the price** at a fixed distance: it moves when the price goes your way, but **never moves back**. That locks in part of your profit while giving the trend room to keep going.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/4/prompt: You bought at 1.0850 with a 30-pip trailing stop. The price rose to 1.0920 and then turned back. Where does the trade close?
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/4/explanation: The stop loss always stays 30 pips below the highest price: 1.0920 − 0.0030 = 1.0890. From the entry to there is 40 pips of profit.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/5/prompt: Same trade: after the 1.0920 high, the trailing stop moved up to 1.0890. Tap the candle that hit the stop loss and closed the trade.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/5/explanation: After the high, this is the first candle whose low reached 1.0890; the trailing stop closed the trade with 40 pips of profit. The next candle went back up: a trailing stop set too tight can sometimes take you out early.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/6/body: In **MetaTrader**, the trailing stop runs on **your own platform**. If the platform is closed, it stops moving, though the last stop loss stays in place. On exchanges, you usually set the distance as a **percentage**. A distance that's too tight means getting knocked out by a normal swing.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/7/prompt: You turned on a MetaTrader trailing stop and shut down your laptop. What happens?
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/7/options/0: The last stop loss stays, but it stops moving
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/7/options/1: The position closes automatically right away
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/7/options/2: The trailing keeps running on the broker's server
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/7/options/3: The stop loss is deleted and the position is unprotected
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/7/explanation: MetaTrader's trailing stop runs on your side. The last stop loss sent to the server stays, but it no longer follows the price. That's why some traders keep their platform running on a VPS.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/8/prompt: Put the management of a buy position in order, from start to finish.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/8/items/0: Enter with a set stop loss and take profit
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/8/items/3: Close when price hits the trailing stop
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/8/explanation: First the risk is set. Once the trade is in profit, the trailing stop locks in part of it, and finally a pullback closes the trade in profit.
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/9/pairs/0/mea: When one fills, the other is canceled
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/9/pairs/1/mea: A stop loss that moves with the price
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/9/pairs/2/mea: A trigger that places a limit order
lessons/orders-u1-l3/steps/9/pairs/3/mea: The order stays active until you cancel it
